description:
About the Team
We're a team from Malaysia tackling the Astronaut Health Monitoring challenge. We're building a tool that helps astronauts far from ground support track their own health and act on it. Our strengths: health and medical knowledge, data analysis, and software development.
summary: Crew Health Monitor is a self-check and emergency guidance app for astronauts on deep space missions, where a delayed signal to Earth means no doctor on call. A tappable body map shows each indicator as green, yellow or red: heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, mood and an estimated bone density. Trends add temperature and sleep, with a 7-day chart for each. A camera scan reads heart rate in under 30 seconds with no extra hardware, processed on the device. When a reading turns red, the app explains in plain language what it means, what to do now and when to contact the flight surgeon. A Quick Aid section gives step-by-step guides with video for CPR, choking and the EpiPen. The app works offline, adapts to phone and desktop, and is built for people with no medical training. It is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

Crew Health Monitor lets an astronaut check their own health in under a minute. A tappable body map shows each tracked indicator as green, yellow or red. Tapping a region opens a plain-language result what the number means, what to do, when to escalate, and the source. If a reading is red, an alert pops up with "Do now" steps and escalation options.

Main features

- Body map with status for heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, mood and estimated bone density

- Camera heart-rate scan (rPPG): about 20-30 seconds, no extra hardware, runs on the device

- 7-day trends for heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood

- Daily check-in with a streak and level to keep the habit

- Learn tab: NASA's five spaceflight hazards and how-to guides for people with no medical training

- Quick Aid: step-by-step guides with video for CPR, helping a choking adult and using an EpiPen

How it works

Readings come from manual entry, the daily check-in, or the camera scan. A rule engine checks each reading against green, yellow and red ranges, for example heart rate above 120 or below 50 is red. The guidance text shows what to do and when to escalate. All of this works with no internet connection.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no framework or build step. Charts and the body map are drawn as SVG. The camera heart rate uses vitallens.js (open source, MIT), vendored with its face model so it runs offline. Sample mission data is read from a CSV file. Video in Quick Aid uses YouTube and needs internet; the written steps do not.

What makes it creative

It treats the astronaut as the first responder. One tap on a body figure replaces forms and menus, the camera scan needs no hardware, and the Quick Aid section turns first-aid training into instructions someone can follow under stress.

What our team considered

- Plain language, because crew may be tired, stressed or untrained

- Offline use, because connection to Earth is delayed

- Honesty about limits: bone density is a model (NASA reports about 1-1.5% loss per month), the camera gives heart rate only, and every guide shows its source

- Safe accuracy: blood pressure green goes up to 129 systolic because validated cuffs can read up to 5 mmHg off (ISO 81060-2)

- Readability and accessibility on any screen size

Impact

In deep space it helps crews self-assess and act without waiting for Earth. On Earth, the same model could bring quick health guidance to remote and underserved communities.

Limits

This is a prototype, not a medical device. Thresholds were set by the team using public medical sources and still need clinical review.
